tour.title: Project Orientation
tour.description: Start here to understand what onixlabs-studio is: a modern cross-platform IDE built on Angular 22 and Electron. The README names the project, while docs/agents.md is the real map — a 34-section architecture guide covering the stack, the feature-first repository layout, the renderer/main runtime seams, coding conventions, and the pre-commit green gate. Skim agents.md now; the rest of this tour walks the seams it describes.

tour.title: Angular Renderer Bootstrap
tour.description: The desktop UI is an Angular app that boots in Electron's renderer process. main.ts bootstraps the Root component with the app config; config.ts assembles zoneless change detection and registers every feature provider plus display, lifecycle, and theme services; and root.ts is the shell component that composes the title, ribbon, content-host, and status strips. Together these three files are the entry point for everything you see on screen.
tour.languageLesson: Angular 22 here runs zoneless — change detection is driven by signals rather than Zone.js. config.ts uses environment providers (provideXxx functions) to compose the app declaratively instead of NgModules.

tour.title: The Electron Main Process
tour.description: Every desktop app has a second entry point: the Node-side backend. electron/main.ts bootstraps a Program lifecycle that creates the BrowserWindow, wires all the IPC managers, applies web-contents security policy, makes GPU rendering decisions, and coordinates a graceful quit. This is the counterpart to the renderer bootstrap from Step 2 — the two processes run side by side and talk over IPC, which is the next thing to understand.

tour.title: The IPC Contract Seam
tour.description: The renderer (Step 2) and main process (Step 3) never share memory — they communicate through a typed IPC bridge. bridge.ts defines the generic invoke/send/on transport that the Electron preload exposes as window.bridge, and channel files like file-channels.ts declare the capability-sliced channel names with their request/response types. This seam is the single most important contract in the codebase: it keeps the UI and backend decoupled yet type-safe.
tour.languageLesson: Each capability (file, lsp, ai, project, task, workspace) gets its own *-channels.ts module pairing a string channel name with a TypeScript request/response type — so both processes compile against one shared contract and drift is caught at build time.

tour.title: The Feature Registry Mechanism
tour.description: onixlabs-studio is feature-first: each feature is a self-contained slice that plugs itself into the shell rather than the shell knowing about features. The feature-registry barrel re-exports the registry service and the provideFeature helper, and provide-feature.ts is the environment-provider factory that registers a feature descriptor at application init. Recall config.ts in Step 2 pulling in 'all feature providers' — this is the mechanism that makes that possible.

tour.title: The Dock & Shell Framework
tour.description: The IDE's window layout is a dockable panel tree, like VS Code or Visual Studio. dock-tree.ts is the pure functional core: immutable operations for finding, tabbing, splitting, docking, moving, reordering, and resizing layout nodes. dock-node.ts is the recursive component that renders a tree node as either a split (with splitters) or a stack (tab group), and dock-panel.ts defines what a dockable panel is. This is the chrome that hosts every feature view from Step 5.
tour.languageLesson: The dock layout separates a pure, immutable tree model (dock-tree.ts — easy to test and reason about) from the recursive rendering component (dock-node.ts). Immutable tree operations return new trees rather than mutating, which pairs naturally with signal-based change detection.

tour.title: Core Renderer State Services
tour.description: Above the dock sit the shared services that hold the IDE's live state. Tabs manages the open-tab collection and the active tab; Documents is the registry tracking open documents, their content, dirty state, file IO, and disk-change reconciliation; StatusBar aggregates owner-keyed contributions into the sorted leading/trailing items shown in the status strip. These are the highest fan-in services in the app — nearly every feature depends on them.

tour.title: Theme & Settings
tour.description: Two cross-cutting services personalize the IDE. Theme resolves light/dark mode and accent color (reading the system preference via matchMedia) and applies CSS custom properties to the document root. Settings is the central store exposing typed reactive accessors and section mutators for application, appearance, editor, workspace, and AI settings, with validation, legacy migration, and persistence. Both were registered back in config.ts (Step 2) and are consumed everywhere.

tour.title: Feature Slice: Code Editor & Monaco
tour.description: Now watch a full feature slice come together. code.feature.ts registers the code-editor view, ribbon, and document panel with the registry from Step 5. The Monaco service handles AMD loading, theme definition, and editor options, while the LSP client manages language-server sessions, document sync, and translates diagnostics into Monaco markers. This slice shows the round-trip: feature to shell to the LSP IPC channel to the main-process language host you'll meet in Step 11.

tour.title: More Feature Slices
tour.description: The same feature pattern repeats across the IDE. terminal.feature.ts registers the terminal view and eagerly initializes agent-terminal capabilities (backed by node-pty in main); markdown.feature.ts provides the Milkdown-based document editor; repository.feature.ts registers the source-control view and ribbon. Each is a thin *.feature.ts provider wiring a view, ribbon, and panels into the shell — proving the architecture from Steps 5-6 scales uniformly.

tour.title: Electron Main-Process Subsystems
tour.description: Behind the IPC seam, the main process runs the real backend that features call into. ai-manager orchestrates AI agent runs, dispatching to the selected provider (Claude Agent SDK, Vercel AI SDK, or Ollama) and mediating tool-permission prompts; lsp-manager spawns language-server child processes and forwards JSON-RPC between renderer and servers; project-system detects a workspace's ecosystem; workspace-manager performs folder/file operations over IPC. These are the depth-1 subsystems wired up by Program in Step 3.

tour.title: Build & Packaging
tour.description: Finally, how it all ships. package.json declares the Electron main entry, the dependency set (Angular 22, Monaco, xterm, node-pty, Claude Agent SDK, LSP tooling), and the scripts that orchestrate Angular builds, esbuild Electron bundling, and distribution. electron-builder.yml turns the compiled main/preload plus the built Angular app into platform installers — dmg/zip for macOS, NSIS for Windows, AppImage for Linux. This closes the loop from source to a shippable cross-platform desktop app.
tour.languageLesson: The two-process app is built in two passes: Angular's compiler produces the renderer bundle, esbuild bundles the Node-side Electron main/preload, and electron-builder packages both into per-OS installers. Separating renderer and main builds mirrors the runtime process split seen throughout this tour.
